data.rationale: FND-020 covers the whole core insight. It converts the ACQ-TH1 arrival time of 06:30 ICT to 07:30 SGT. It adds 45 minutes of matching and 15 minutes of report generation to reach about 08:30 SGT, which misses the NFR-8 deadline of 08:00 SGT. It also notes that 2027 volume makes the gap worse. Its cited sections (16.1, 16.2 and 2.2) and NFR-8 overlap the flaw's location. The other findings in the location hint cover unrelated defects: latency, RPO, the state machine, CVC retention and network tokens.

Only FND-050 is about this flaw. It cites section 9.3 and the 10,000 WCU claim. It names the hot merchant_id key, notes that 4 KB response bodies and LSI writes add write cost, and raises the item-collection size limit. It does not say outright that the real limit is 1,000 WCU, which is for the scoring step to weigh. The other idempotency findings cover different defects: FND-001 (Redis key scope) and FND-024 (concurrency and crash recovery).

FND-029 states the core insight directly. In Section 13.1 the Fraud Hook detokenises the PAN using the Card Adapter's service role and sends it to FRV-1. That contradicts the out-of-scope classification in 12.2, Principle P2 and the 12.1 detokenise restriction, so the CDE scoping that NFR-5 relies on is wrong. It also says PAN would go to a vendor whose PCI status is not established. No other finding fits. FND-052 is the fail-open distractor, FND-016 is about phase sequencing, and FND-001 is about idempotency.

FND-019 is the clear match. It cites NFR-4's requirement of zero RPO on region loss, says Section 20.2 replicates asynchronously with lag under one second, and concludes that commits in the lag window are lost. That covers all three credit items (c1, c2 and c3) at the flaw's location. FND-044 is only a weak secondary candidate. It cites 20.2 and NFR-4 and the lack of cross-region replication, but its defect is the HSM single point of failure and the missing Vault and HSM regional DR, not the RPO contradiction. The other hinted findings (FND-005, FND-036, FND-020 and FND-028) are about different defects.

Only FND-028 is about this defect. It cites 12.4 and NFR-6 and says the cited clauses 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow storage only before authorization. It also says keeping SAD after authorization is not allowed, even encrypted, and that keeping the CVC until settlement or up to 72 hours puts the assessment at risk. The other findings cover unrelated issues.

FND-045 states the core insight. MFA is optional for Finance users, a Finance user can change the payout bank account, and the only confirmation goes to the user who made the change. That means one phished password can divert the merchant's payouts with no alert. It cites 18.2, 18.3, 18.4 and FR-13. FND-036 overlaps only through section 24, and it is about network-token readiness, a different defect. None of the other findings is about merchant authentication or payout account changes.

FND-005 is the best match for F05. It covers all three credit items: the claim in 21.1 that fewer than 1% of payments cascade conflicts with the 3.8% retryable rate in 10.5. A timeout-triggered cascade adds 2,500 ms. As a result, the cascade tail falls inside the p99 and NFR-2's 1,500 ms limit fails. FND-043 is a weak secondary candidate only. It cites the 2,500 ms timeout in 11.2, but its defect is double authorization from discarding late approvals, not p99 latency. The remaining hinted findings (FND-019, FND-020, FND-028) concern RPO, reconciliation timing and CVC retention, which are different defects.

FND-039 is the only finding about this defect. It cites Section 19.1 (all primary data in ap-southeast-1) and NFR-7 (privacy laws only). It points out that the design assumes cross-border processing is allowed in every market, including under local payment-system regulators such as domestic QR rails, and it calls for legal confirmation of any localisation obligation. It does not single out Indonesia, but the main point matches. FND-044 and FND-019 also cite Section 20.2, but they are about HSM and DR resilience and about RPO, not data residency.

FND-001 explicitly states that the Redis key idem:resp:{idempotency_key} has no merchant scope (breaking P3), that collisions are likely because merchants use order or invoice IDs, and that one merchant receives another's stored payment object. It also notes the skipped request-hash check. None of the other findings addresses the Redis key's missing merchant scope: FND-024 covers concurrency and crash recovery, FND-050 covers DynamoDB hot keys and FND-019 covers DR rebuild.

FND-044 states the core insight directly. It says there is one HSM in ap-southeast-1a, that every detokenise unwrap happens without caching, and that card authorization stops if that HSM or AZ is lost. It also notes that the 1,500 TPS trigger is never reached at about 1,100 TPS peak, and it cites NFR-3. No other finding covers the HSM topology. FND-029 and FND-036 only touch the same sections on other topics: detokenise scope and network tokens.

FND-026 is the only finding about this defect. It says FR-8's '2%' and Section 10.3's 'default 2' have no unit, so the tolerance could mean 2 percentage points or a 2% relative drop, and that the two readings route differently. It cites FR-8, 2.1 and 10.3, and it quotes the weekly merchant-level realised-rate review. The other findings that overlap the flaw's location raise different defects: scheme limits (FND-025), token requestor approval (FND-036), phase sequencing (FND-016) and idempotency (FND-024).

FND-043 is the only finding that describes this defect. It cites 11.1 and 11.2 and FR-7 and quotes the anchor claim. It says a 2,500 ms timeout triggers a cascade, a late approval is thrown away, and the hold at the first acquirer is left live and never reversed, so the cardholder can be authorized twice. It also notes the ledger-only argument ignores what the cardholder sees. FND-005 mentions timeout-triggered cascades, but only as a latency problem. The other hinted findings deal with idempotency, scheme limits, RPO or network tokens, not this defect.

FND-036 makes the same point as the key flaw. Section 24 confirms network tokens from launch, and Section 27 and Phase 3 rate them ready. But Backlog item 2 says the TRID/TSP application has not been submitted and certification has not started. So the decision and the readiness ratings depend on an external dependency that is still open. The other hinted findings are about different defects: fraud fail-open (FND-052), cohort sequencing (FND-016) and missing scheme reattempt limits (FND-025).

FND-024 is the only finding that states this flaw's core insight. It cites FR-5 and §26.1 and says FR-5 requires correct handling when duplicates arrive concurrently. It then points out that the acceptance test resends only after the first response, so it never tests the concurrent path or the conditional-put race. It also covers the 409 path and crash recovery. The other findings that touch FR-5 or §9 (FND-001, FND-019, FND-050) describe different defects.

The finding states the full timing argument. It does the time-zone conversion: "ACQ-TH1 delivers at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT". It adds up the run: "45 minutes of matching plus 15 minutes of report generation at 2025 volume, so reports land around 08:30 SGT", and concludes that "NFR-8 ... fails by construction". It also covers growth: "even before 2027 volume roughly doubles the load". It cites sections 16.2, 16.1 and 2.2 and NFR-8, which overlap the key's location. It does not just criticise batch reconciliation in general, so the distractor note does not apply.

It cites sections 2.2 and 20.2 and NFR-4, so the location overlaps the flaw's. Its focus is the single CloudHSM in ap-southeast-1a: "Losing that AZ or that HSM stops all card tokenisation". It also says that "Section 20.2 also gives no cross-region plan for the Vault store or the HSM, so after a regional failover cards cannot be processed." That is a gap in availability and failover coverage. The finding never says that NFR-4 requires RPO = 0 on region loss. It never says that Aurora Global Database replicates asynchronously, and it never concludes that commits in the lag window would be lost. It quotes the line that MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated, but only as context for its HSM and Vault argument. It does not use that line to show an RPO contradiction. "Puts NFR-3 and NFR-4 at risk" is generic. This is the same area with a different mechanism, so it scores RELATED.

data.doc_passage: On completion of a request, the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL. data.label: SUPPORTED

data.rationale: The document backs up every part of the finding's premise. Section 9.2 builds the Redis key from the idempotency key alone, with no merchant_id. On a hit, it returns the stored response immediately, before the hash comparison. That comparison only happens on the DynamoDB path. Section 24 repeats the key as idem:resp:{key}. P3 scopes idempotency to the pair (merchant, key). Section 9.1 says merchants' order and invoice IDs are accepted as keys. FR-5 requires HTTP 422 when a key is reused with a different body.

data.doc_passage: The CVC is required for the initial customer-initiated authorization and, at several acquirers, for each re-presentation of the credential during a cascade and for incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions). This is permitted by PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2, which allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document keeps the CVC encrypted in the Vault after authorization, until settlement or for at most 72 hours, so it can be re-presented in cascades and incremental authorizations. It justifies this by saying PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.
data.rationale: The finding describes and quotes the document accurately. Section 12.4 keeps the CVC encrypted until the payment is SETTLED or for at most 72 hours, gives cascades and incremental authorizations as the reason, and cites PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 as allowing this. NFR-6 says sensitive authentication data is stored encrypted and deleted at settlement. Section 24 records the confirmed decision "Encrypted in Vault until settlement, max 72 hours." Section 11.2 also has cascades retrieving the CVC from the Vault. Whether the reviewer reads PCI DSS correctly is a question about the standard, not about what this document says, so it is outside this check.

data.doc_passage: The Vault's KEKs are held in an AWS CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. CloudHSM takes automatic daily backups of the cluster to S3, from which a new HSM can be created in any AZ. A second HSM will be added to the cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS.
data.label: SUPPORTED

Its trigger for a second HSM (1,500 TPS of sustained card volume) is above the projected peak card volume of about 1,100 TPS, and its cross-region DR plan does not cover the Vault or the HSM.
data.rationale:
The document backs every part of this finding:
- **One HSM:** Section 12.3 says there is one HSM in ap-southeast-1a, restorable from daily backups, with a second HSM added only above 1,500 TPS of sustained card volume. Section 24 repeats "one HSM at launch".
- **No DEK caching:** Section 12.1 says each detokenise call unwraps the DEK inside the HSM and DEKs are not cached.
- **Peak card volume:** Section 1 sets peak at 2,000 TPS with a 55% card share. That gives about 1,100 card TPS, which never reaches the 1,500 TPS trigger.
- **No cross-region plan for the Vault or HSM:** Section 20.2 covers only Aurora Global Database, MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache. Neither it nor Section 19.1 mentions replicating or recovering the Vault store or the CloudHSM in ap-southeast-3.

data.doc_passage: Because each attempt carries its own attempt_id and the previous attempt did not succeed, cascading cannot create a duplicate charge: the ledger records only the approved attempt. Responses that arrive for an attempt after its 2,500 ms timeout are logged against the attempt and discarded.

It also says late responses are logged and discarded, and argues that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the ledger records only the approved attempt. It gives no mechanism for reversing a late approval at the first acquirer.

Section 11.2 says late responses are logged and discarded, and bases the no-duplicate-charge claim on the ledger. The document has no void or reversal step for a late approval at the first acquirer. The stuck-payment sweeper (20.3) only resolves payments that are still in AUTHORISING. Reconciliation (16.2) matches settlement lines, so an authorization that is never captured would not show up there.

CREATED -> REQUIRES_ACTION | AUTHORISING | FAILED | CANCELLED
REQUIRES_ACTION -> AUTHORISING | CANCELLED (expiry)
AUTHORISING -> AUTHORISED | SUCCEEDED | FAILED
AUTHORISED -> CAPTURED | CANCELLED (void or auth expiry)
CAPTURED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SUCCEEDED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
SETTLED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED
PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED

Other sections need these flows: Section 16.2 moves matched payments to SETTLED, FR-1 allows partial captures, and wallet or 3DS declines must be handled. FR-2 forbids any transition not on the list.
data.rationale: Section 7.2 gives PARTIALLY_REFUNDED only one way out (to REFUNDED), and REFUNDED has no way out at all, so neither can reach SETTLED. REQUIRES_ACTION can only move to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED, so it cannot go to FAILED. CAPTURED cannot move back to CAPTURED. Meanwhile, Section 16.2 says "Matched payments transition to SETTLED", FR-1 calls for partial captures, and FR-2 says "only the transitions listed there shall be permitted." So what the finding says the document contains, and leaves out, is accurate. One weaker point: an "authorize-and-hold-capture" outcome could arguably be covered by the existing AUTHORISED state. That doesn't change the main premise.

data.doc_passage: FR-5: "...shall return the identical response, including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently." §9.1: "While the first request is in flight, a duplicate receives HTTP 409 request_in_progress with Retry-After: 1." §26.1 FR-5: "Send a create-payment request; after its response is received, resend the identical request with the same Idempotency-Key."
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: FR-5 requires an identical response even for concurrent duplicates, but Section 9.1 returns HTTP 409 to in-flight duplicates, and the FR-5 acceptance test only resends after the first response arrives, so the concurrent path is never tested.
data.rationale: All three quotes appear in the document exactly as cited. FR-5 asks for an identical response even when duplicates arrive concurrently. Section 9.1 instead returns 409 to a duplicate that arrives while the first request is still in flight. The FR-5 acceptance test only resends after the first response has come back, so it never tests the concurrent case or the race on the conditional put. Section 9.2 does say a crashed pod's IN_PROGRESS lock is cleared by the stuck-payment sweeper. Section 20.3 describes that sweeper as finding payments stuck in AUTHORISING, and adds that it "also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS." The finding's claim that a crash before any payment row exists leaves the key blocked is an inference from these sections, not something the document states. The finding's central premise is accurate.

data.doc_passage: All primary data stores (Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, MSK, S3 intake and archive buckets) are in ap-southeast-1. The Aurora Global Database secondary in ap-southeast-3 (Jakarta) is used for disaster recovery only (Section 20).

Although NFR-7 names five national data-protection laws, the document records no cross-border transfer mechanism, data-localisation analysis or regulator view.

Section 20.2 confirms that Aurora Global Database replicates the payments and ledger cluster to ap-southeast-3. NFR-7 lists the five laws, but it only mentions purpose limitation, retention limits and access logging. Its validation step (DPO sign-off and mapping each field to a purpose and retention period) does not cover cross-border transfer. I searched for transfer mechanisms, data localisation, cross-border data rules and payment-system regulators such as central banks or QR-rail operators, including synonyms, and found none of them anywhere in the document.

data.doc_passage: At routing time, the engine compares the approval prior of the lowest-cost acquirer against that of the highest-approval acquirer and applies the cost preference when the difference is within the configured tolerance (default 2).
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The FR-8 routing tolerance has no defined unit ("2%" in FR-8, "default 2" in Section 10.3), so it is unclear whether it means percentage points or a relative drop, and the FR-8 test only checks that the selected acquirer matches a preset expectation, not the authorization-rate bound.
data.rationale: FR-8 says the cost preference applies "unless doing so reduces the expected authorization rate by more than 2%". Section 10.3 says "configured tolerance (default 2)" and Section 24 says "cost-preferred within 2 tolerance". None of these gives a unit, and the document never says "percentage points" or "relative" anywhere, so the absence claim holds. The FR-8 test in Section 26.1 only requires that "the selected acquirer matches the expected choice" and does not measure the authorization rate. Section 10.2 does say the default weights emphasise cost. Section 10.3 does say the ranking "is subject to FR-8", which partly answers the precedence point, but that is secondary and does not undercut the central premise.

items.rationale: Section 9.2 states the Redis fast-path key is idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, with no merchant identity in it. This establishes that the cache is keyed only on the idempotency key.

On a hit, the stored response is returned immediately without touching DynamoDB, which is where request_hash is stored. This establishes that a hit gets no further check, including no hash comparison.
Section 9.1 explicitly accepts merchants' own order or invoice identifiers as keys, which supports the claim that two merchants can easily use the same key.

The source passages establish each premise: the key carries no merchant ID (EV-001), a hit returns immediately and skips the stored hash (EV-002), and order IDs are accepted as keys while reuse with a different body should get 422 (EV-003). Together these support cross-merchant serving and the skipped 422 rule.
P3 states that idempotency is scoped to the pair (merchant, key). This establishes the principle the claim says is broken.
FR-5 requires that a reused key with a different request body be rejected with HTTP 422. This establishes the requirement the claim says is broken.

The basic mechanism follows from the source passages: a merchant-less Redis key, a hit with no hash check, and accepted order-ID keys. However, the figure of 15,000 merchants and the conclusion that a collision is 'likely within 24 hours' appear in none of the source passages.

The shared namespace and the bypassed 422 rule are supported by the source passages. However, '15,000 merchants', 'sequential order IDs' and 'near-certain' collisions are not established by them. The passages only say order or invoice IDs are accepted.

The passage sits just before 13.2, so it is Section 13.1. It says the Fraud Hook gets the PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation using the Card Adapter client library and service role. It also says FRV-1's velocity graph is keyed on the full card number, which means the PAN is sent to FRV-1.
The Section 12.2 table lists the Fraud Hook as 'Out of scope' on the basis 'Token, BIN, last 4 only', as the claim says.
Backlog item 4 is 'FRV-1 contract - data processing agreement and SLA finalisation', so the DPA and SLA are still pending. It is cited only for that part of the claim, not for FRV-1's PCI status.
The passage comes before 12.2, so it is Section 12.1. It says 'Only the Card Adapter's service identity may call detokenise', which establishes the restriction the claim cites.

Together, the source passages show a contradiction: the Fraud Hook gets the PAN by detokenising, yet 12.2 scopes it out as token, BIN and last 4 only. The Card Adapter's 'Transmits PAN to acquirers' basis suggests the same logic should apply to the Fraud Hook.
